#!/bin/bash
# PreToolUse hook for the Bash tool — blocks the ugrep DFA-explosion pattern.
#
# THE HAZARD. Since Claude Code v2.1.117 the Bash-tool shell snapshot shadows
# `grep` with a shell FUNCTION that re-execs the ~300MB `claude.exe` binary as
# `ARGV0=ugrep ... -G` (ugrep 7.5.0 is embedded in the CLI; there is no `ugrep`
# on PATH). So a plain `grep` from the Bash tool is NOT GNU grep. Upstream bug:
# https://github.com/anthropics/claude-code/issues/54394 (open as of 2026-08-22).
#
# ugrep's default POSIX engine (RE/flex) compiles the pattern to a DFA BEFORE
# matching, and linear-time matchers must expand bounded repetitions away. Two
# counted repetitions over a wide character class around a literal make the DFA
# track the cross product of both counters — construction then allocates
# without bound: ~70-130 MB/s, no output, no termination, no SIGPIPE (it never
# emits a match, so a downstream `head` never kills it).
#
# 2026-08-22: Arwen ran
#     grep -o -i '[^<>]\{0,120\}retry[^<>]\{0,120\}' design.html
# on a 116KB minified HTML file (longest line 91,000 chars). One process reached
# 8.9G (rss+swap) inside the session's own scope, pushed it past MemoryHigh=8G
# with the 2G swap cap full, and livelocked the WHOLE cgroup — including the
# claude process — in mem_cgroup_handle_over_high for ~40 minutes. The session
# itself was innocent at ~800MB. GNU grep runs the identical pattern in 4.0s /
# 13MB and returns the right answer.
#
# THE DISCRIMINATOR (measured on that file, each in a hard-capped test.slice
# scope — see docs/host-gotchas.md for the full table):
#   [^<>]{0,120}retry[^<>]{0,120}   RUNAWAY      two wide bounds, both sides
#   .{0,120}retry.{0,120}           RUNAWAY      `.` counts as wide
#   \w{0,120}retry\w{0,120}         RUNAWAY
#   .{0,60}re.{0,60}try.{0,60}      RUNAWAY      three bounds
#   [^<>]{0,120}retry               ok    6MB    ONE bound is harmless
#   [0-9]{0,120}retry[0-9]{0,120}   ok    7MB    narrow class is harmless
#   [^<>]{0,25}retry[^<>]{0,25}     ok    7MB    small bound is harmless
#   bound sweep, both sides: {0,20} 6MB · {0,30} 184MB · {0,40}+ RUNAWAY
# So the trip is: >=2 counted repetitions whose max is >=32. Class width is NOT
# tested statically — it is not reliably decidable from the command text, and
# the false-positive cost is one extra flag while the false-negative cost is a
# frozen box. Deliberately NOT part of the rule: the alternation shape from
# issue #54394 (`"a":"[^"]*"|"b":"[^"]*"|...`) measured clean at 7MB here, so
# guarding it would be pure false-positive noise on this ugrep version.
#
# EXEMPT (all measured safe, all leave the caller a working escape):
#   -P / --perl-regexp   PCRE2 backtracks instead of building a DFA — 7MB
#   command grep         bypasses the function shim entirely
#   /bin/grep, /usr/bin/grep, any path-qualified grep — real GNU grep, 13MB
#   git grep             git's own matcher
#   rg / ripgrep         never matched here to begin with
# Only BARE `grep` is shimmed (the snapshot shadows exactly `find` and `grep`),
# so `egrep`/`fgrep` are real binaries and are not guarded.
#
# ANALYSIS IS WHOLE-COMMAND, NOT PER-SEGMENT. An earlier draft split on
# | && ; & and judged each segment. Three defects, all measured: a `;` or `&`
# INSIDE the pattern ([^&<>]{0,120}x[^&<>]{0,120}) split the counters apart and
# the runaway sailed through; a grep that is not the first word of its segment
# (`do grep`, `if grep`, `time grep`, a line continuation) was never examined;
# and the cost was ~7ms per line of command, 2.25s on a 300-line heredoc.
# Counting bounds across the whole command first is cheaper (one pass, exits in
# ~3 forks for the 99% case that has no large bounds at all) and strictly
# harder to evade. It over-approximates — a command with two large bounds
# somewhere and an unrelated grep elsewhere is treated as dangerous — which is
# the right direction to be wrong in, because the remedy is a safe rewrite.
#
# Fails OPEN if the command can't be read or jq is missing — a guard that
# cannot parse must not wedge every Bash call (matches slot-test-guard).

BOUND_MIN="${UGREP_GUARD_BOUND_MIN:-32}"   # a counted max >= this is "large"
COUNT_MIN="${UGREP_GUARD_COUNT_MIN:-2}"    # this many large counts = explosion
PREFIX_SIG='grep() { command '                # our own rewrite marker

INPUT=$(cat)
CMD=$(printf '%s' "$INPUT" | jq -r '.tool_input.command // empty' 2>/dev/null)
[ -z "$CMD" ] && exit 0

# Idempotence: never re-wrap our own output.
case "$CMD" in "$PREFIX_SIG"*) exit 0 ;; esac

# ── Fast path ───────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
# One pass over the whole command. Handles ERE `{0,120}` / `{120}` and BRE
# `\{0,120\}`; ignores open-ended `{5,}` (an unbounded loop needs no counter,
# so it cannot blow the DFA up). Almost every command exits here.
NBOUNDS=$(printf '%s' "$CMD" \
  | grep -oE '\\?\{[0-9]*(,[0-9]*)?\\?\}' \
  | sed -E 's/\\//g; s/[{}]//g' \
  | awk -F, -v min="$BOUND_MIN" '
      { max = (NF > 1 ? $2 : $1) }
      max ~ /^[0-9]+$/ && max + 0 >= min { c++ }
      END { print c + 0 }')
[ "${NBOUNDS:-0}" -ge "$COUNT_MIN" ] || exit 0

# ── Strip quoted spans and heredoc bodies ───────────────────────────
# Detection must look at words this shell will actually EXECUTE. A matcher
# name sitting inside a quoted payload or a heredoc is DATA, not an
# invocation: it belongs to `ssh host "..."`, `bash -c "..."`, a script being
# written with `cat > f <<EOF`, or a `herdr agent prompt` string. Judging
# those refused perfectly good commands - writing this hook's own test
# harness was blocked by this hook three times, which is how the
# false-positive rate got measured. The pattern text stays visible to the
# bound counter above (patterns ARE quoted); only the token and flag scanning
# below runs on the blanked text, so a real unquoted invocation is still
# caught. Quote state is carried ACROSS lines and honours backslash escapes
# inside double quotes, because a desync would blank real code and turn a
# false positive into a false NEGATIVE; heredoc terminators are matched
# allowing <<- tab-stripping and trailing whitespace. Fails open to the raw
# command if awk is unavailable.
BLANKED=$(printf '%s' "$CMD" | awk '
BEGIN { inh = 0; q = 0; qc = ""; dash = 0; ansic = 0 }
{
  line = $0
  if (inh) {
    t = line
    if (dash) { sub(/^[ \t]+/, "", t) }
    sub(/[ \t]+$/, "", t)
    if (t == term) inh = 0
    print ""; next
  }
  out = ""; n = length(line)
  for (i = 1; i <= n; i++) {
    c = substr(line, i, 1)
    # A backslash OUTSIDE quotes escapes the next character, so `echo it\'"'"'s`
    # never opens a string. Without this the apostrophe opened one awk-side that
    # bash never opened, and every following line was blanked — hiding a real
    # grep. Emitting the escaped char keeps `\grep` visible to detection.
    if (q == 0 && c == "\\") { out = out " " substr(line, i+1, 1); i++; continue }
    # A `#` starting a word begins a comment: the rest of the line is not code.
    # This matters because quote state is now carried ACROSS lines, so an
    # apostrophe in a comment ("# we don'"'"'t want ugrep here") would otherwise
    # open a string that swallows the remainder of the command.
    if (q == 0 && c == "#" && (i == 1 || substr(line, i-1, 1) ~ /[ \t;&|(]/)) { break }
    if (q == 1 && c == "\\" && (qc == "\"" || ansic)) { out = out "  "; i++; continue }
    if (q == 0 && (c == "'"'"'" || c == "\"")) { q = 1; qc = c; ansic = (c == "'"'"'" && i > 1 && substr(line, i-1, 1) == "$"); out = out " "; continue }
    if (q == 1 && c == qc)                        { q = 0; qc = ""; ansic = 0; out = out " "; continue }
    if (q == 1)                                   { out = out " "; continue }
    out = out c
  }
  if (q == 0 && match(out, /<<-?/)) {
    pos = RSTART + RLENGTH
    dash = (substr(out, RSTART, RLENGTH) ~ /-$/)
    if (substr(out, pos, 1) != "<") {
      rest = substr(line, pos)
      sub(/^[ \t]*/, "", rest)
      sub(/^[\047\"]/, "", rest)
      if (match(rest, /^[A-Za-z_][A-Za-z0-9_]*/)) {
        term = substr(rest, RSTART, RLENGTH); inh = 1
      }
    }
  }
  print out
}
' 2>/dev/null) || BLANKED="$CMD"
# `eval` is the one payload that is NOT data: it runs in THIS shell, so its
# quoted contents must stay visible to detection. Test the BLANKED text, not
# the raw command — an `eval` that is itself inside a heredoc (a deploy script
# being written) or inside an ssh payload is data like everything else, and
# keying off the raw text let it switch blanking off for the whole command.
if printf '%s' "$BLANKED" | grep -Eq '(^|[^A-Za-z0-9_.-])eval([[:space:]]|$)'; then
  BLANKED="$CMD"
fi
[ -n "$BLANKED" ] || BLANKED="$CMD"

# ── Which greps are in play? ────────────────────────────────────────────────
# Neutralise the invocations that never reach the shim, then see whether a bare
# `grep` word survives. Only a bare `grep` resolves to the shell function;
# `command grep`, `git grep` and any path-qualified grep are real matchers.
STRIPPED=$(printf '%s' "$BLANKED" | sed -E '
  s#(^|[^A-Za-z0-9_.-])(command[[:space:]]+grep|git[[:space:]]+grep)#\1_SAFEGREP_#g
  s#[A-Za-z0-9_./-]*/grep#_SAFEGREP_#g')
printf '%s' "$STRIPPED" | grep -Eq '(^|[^A-Za-z0-9_.-])grep([[:space:]]|$)' || exit 0

# Flag zone = from each bare `grep` up to the first quote OR shell
# metacharacter, whichever comes first — i.e. that grep's OWN argv and nothing
# else. Two distinct bugs are being avoided here. Stopping at the quote keeps
# the PATTERN TEXT out: without it `grep -o '.{0,120} -P .{0,120}'`
# false-exempts and `'.{0,120} -r .{0,120}'` false-trips the recursive branch
# (both measured). Stopping at a metacharacter keeps DOWNSTREAM COMMANDS out:
# with an unquoted pattern there is no quote to stop at, so the zone ran to
# end-of-line and `grep -oE PAT f | xargs -P 4 sh` false-exempted on xargs's
# -P, while an innocent later `ls -R` or `cp -r` false-tripped the veto.
ZONES=$(printf '%s' "$STRIPPED" | grep -oE '(^|[^A-Za-z0-9_.-])grep[^'"'"'"|;&<>()]*' || true)

# Recursive anywhere in the command => refuse; see the rewrite rationale below.
IS_RECURSIVE=0
printf '%s' "$ZONES" | grep -Eq -- '(^|[[:space:]])(-[A-Za-z]*[rR][A-Za-z]*|--recursive|--dereference-recursive)([[:space:]]|$)' && IS_RECURSIVE=1
# -d recurse / --directories=recurse walk directories exactly like -r, so
# they must veto the rewrite too — otherwise a recursive search gets its
# result set silently changed, which is the one outcome this hook refuses.
printf '%s' "$ZONES" | grep -Eq -- '(^|[[:space:]])(-d[[:space:]]*|--directories=)recurse' && IS_RECURSIVE=1

# Exempt only if EVERY bare grep already selects PCRE2 (no DFA, measured 7MB).
NZONES=$(printf '%s' "$ZONES" | grep -c . || true)
NPERL=$(printf '%s' "$ZONES" | grep -cE -- '(^|[[:space:]])(-[A-Za-z]*P[A-Za-z]*|--perl-regexp)([[:space:]]|=|$)' || true)
[ "${NZONES:-0}" -gt 0 ] && [ "${NPERL:-0}" -eq "${NZONES:-0}" ] && exit 0

# ── Remediation ─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
# Same principle as slot-test-guard -> capbuild: do not just refuse the work,
# route it somewhere safe. The difference is that a build is LEGITIMATELY heavy
# and needs a cgroup, whereas a grep is legitimately light — the weight here is
# purely a defect in one engine. So the safe route is not "run the broken thing
# in a box", it is "use the engine that is not broken": GNU grep answers the
# incident query in 0.4s at 13MB, against unbounded growth from ugrep.
#
# PreToolUse can rewrite the command (hookSpecificOutput.updatedInput), so the
# repair is applied FOR the caller rather than asked of them — no wasted turn,
# and it does not depend on the agent cooperating. Prepending a `grep()`
# function redefines the shim AFTER the shell snapshot has been sourced, so it
# wins for every grep in the command, including inside pipelines (verified).
# The Bash tool runs a FRESH bash per call, so the override cannot leak into a
# later call, and shell functions are not exported, so `xargs grep` /
# `find -exec grep` / `bash -c 'grep'` never reach the shim to begin with.
#
# THE REWRITE IS ALL-OR-NOTHING, AND RECURSION ANYWHERE VETOES IT. The prefix
# redefines `grep` for the WHOLE command, so it also converts any OTHER grep in
# the same command. The shim passes ugrep `--ignore-files --hidden
# --exclude-dir=.git`, and `--ignore-files` (gitignore awareness) has NO GNU
# equivalent — so converting an unrelated `grep -rn TODO src/` riding along in
# the same command silently starts matching inside .git/ and node_modules/.
# Measured: same command, ugrep 2 hits vs GNU 4 hits including .git and a
# vendored file. A silent change to a result set is worse than the memory bug
# this hook exists to prevent, so if ANY grep in the command is recursive the
# whole command is refused with guidance instead of rewritten.
#
# `-I` is part of the shim's flag set and is NOT a GNU default: without it GNU
# prints "binary file matches" and exits 0 where ugrep prints nothing and exits
# 1, which inverts `if grep -q ...`. So the rewrite pins `-I` to keep the exit
# status honest. (GNU supports -P too, so a mixed command containing a `-P`
# grep still rewrites correctly.)
GNU_GREP=""
for c in /bin/grep /usr/bin/grep; do [ -x "$c" ] && { GNU_GREP="$c"; break; }; done

WHY='`grep` from the Bash tool is NOT GNU grep. Claude Code (>=2.1.117) shadows it with a shell function that re-execs its own binary as the embedded ugrep, whose POSIX engine builds a DFA up front and expands counted repetitions. Two or more counted maxima over a wide class make it track the cross product and allocate WITHOUT BOUND — ~100MB/s, no output, and no SIGPIPE to stop it because it never emits a match, so a downstream `head` will not save you. On 2026-08-22 exactly this shape (`grep -o '"'"'[^<>]\{0,120\}retry[^<>]\{0,120\}'"'"' design.html` over a minified HTML file with a 91,000-char line) reached 8.9G in ONE process, blew past the session'"'"'s 8G MemoryHigh with its swap cap full, and livelocked the whole session cgroup for 40 minutes. Upstream: anthropics/claude-code#54394. Measured on that file: GNU grep 0.4s/13MB with the correct answer; ugrep unbounded. Single counted repetitions, narrow classes like [0-9], and maxima under 32 are all fine and are never touched here.'

if [ -n "$GNU_GREP" ] && [ "$IS_RECURSIVE" -eq 0 ]; then
  NEW_CMD="grep() { command $GNU_GREP -I \"\$@\"; }; $CMD"
  MSG="ugrep-guard: rerouted the grep(s) in this command to GNU grep ($GNU_GREP -I). $WHY Only the regex ENGINE changed, so the match result is the same; the one difference is binary files, which -I keeps skipped exactly as the shim does. Write it this way yourself next time: /bin/grep, -P, or rg."
  printf '%s' "$INPUT" | jq -c --arg c "$NEW_CMD" --arg m "$MSG" \
    '{hookSpecificOutput:{hookEventName:"PreToolUse",updatedInput:(.tool_input + {command:$c})},systemMessage:$m}'
  exit 0
fi

if [ "$IS_RECURSIVE" -eq 1 ]; then
  REASON="Refusing this command: it has two or more large counted repetitions AND a RECURSIVE grep. $WHY It is not auto-rerouted to GNU grep the way a single-file grep is, because the reroute redefines grep for the WHOLE command: the shim passes ugrep --ignore-files --hidden --exclude-dir=.git, and --ignore-files has no GNU equivalent, so a recursive grep would silently start matching inside .git/ and node_modules/ — a different result set, quietly. Pick explicitly: rg 'PATTERN' (respects ignore files, no DFA blowup) is usually what you want; or grep -rP if your pattern is PCRE-compatible, which keeps ugrep's exact file selection and only changes the regex dialect (note -P reads {0,120} as PCRE, so a BRE '"'"'\{0,120\}'"'"' becomes '"'"'{0,120}'"'"'); or $GNU_GREP -r with your own --exclude-dir flags. If the recursive grep is a separate, innocent part of a compound command, just run it as its own Bash call."
else
  REASON="Refusing a grep with two or more large counted repetitions, and no GNU grep was found at /bin/grep or /usr/bin/grep to reroute it to. $WHY Use rg, or add -P to select PCRE2 (which backtracks instead of building a DFA), rewriting any BRE '"'"'\{0,120\}'"'"' as '"'"'{0,120}'"'"'."
fi
printf '{"decision": "block", "reason": %s}\n' "$(printf '%s' "$REASON" | jq -Rs .)"
exit 0

#!/bin/bash
# PreToolUse hook for the Bash tool.
#
# The bashrc `pnpm()/next()/vitest()/jest()` wrappers only guard *interactive*
# shells. Claude runs Bash-tool commands via non-interactive `bash -c`, which
# does NOT source ~/.bashrc — so the wrappers never fire on the path that
# OOM'd the box on 2026-06-07 (a Claude session ran a bare `vitest` pool,
# 10.7G, that killed user@1000.service). This hook is the front-line for that
# path: it refuses bare dev-server / test-runner / build invocations and tells
# Claude to route them through `slot`/`capbuild` (→ dev.slice 12G cap).
# (A bare `pnpm build`→`next build` + parallel `tsc --noEmit` swap-thrashed
# every session for ~80min on 2026-06-18 — builds are as heavy as test pools.)
# claude.slice is the
# cgroup catch-all behind it; this hook stops the obvious cases up front.
#
# Design: split the command line into pipeline/list segments and judge each
# independently, AFTER stripping leading env-var assignments, an `env` prefix,
# and any binary path prefix. That closes the cheap bypasses a single anchored
# regex left open (`CI=1 pnpm test`, `./node_modules/.bin/vitest`,
# `slot pnpm dev & pnpm test`).
#
# Allowed:
#   - a segment routed through `slot ...`            (dev.slice, soft cap)
#   - a segment routed through `capbuild ...`        (hard MemoryMax cgroup)
#   - `systemd-run ... --slice=dev|claude|test.slice` (explicitly capped)
#
# NOT allowed — by design there is NO unbounded escape from the Bash tool.
# `FORCE_BARE=1` is honored ONLY by the interactive-shell wrappers in
# ~/.bashrc (a human at a prompt), never here. An autonomous agent in a
# /loop used `FORCE_BARE=1 npm test` as its default path and swap-thrashed
# every session on 2026-06-11 — because the old block message literally
# coached the bypass. The *channel* separates human from agent: humans type
# in an interactive shell, agents arrive through this non-interactive hook.
# So the hatch lives in bashrc; this hook has none. The remediation message
# points at `capbuild`, which gets the agent its test output AND a hard cap.
#
# Fails OPEN if the command can't be read or jq is missing — a guard that
# can't parse must not wedge every Bash call (matches lsp-memory-guard).

INPUT=$(cat)
CMD=$(printf '%s' "$INPUT" | jq -r '.tool_input.command // empty' 2>/dev/null)
[ -z "$CMD" ] && exit 0

# Runner/action fragments (matched after a segment is normalized to start at
# the bare binary name).
PKG_RUNNERS='pnpm|npm|yarn|turbo|bun'
PKG_FLAGS='run|exec|--filter=[^[:space:]]+|-w|--workspace-root|--silent'
PKG_ACTIONS='dev|start|test|test:[^[:space:]]+|build|build:[^[:space:]]+|vitest|jest'
BIN_RUNNERS='vitest|jest|mocha|ava'

# Echoes "x" if the normalized segment $1 is a bare dangerous runner.
_is_bad() {
  local s="$1"
  printf '%s' "$s" | grep -Eq "^($PKG_RUNNERS)([[:space:]]+($PKG_FLAGS))*[[:space:]]+($PKG_ACTIONS)([[:space:]]|\$)" && { echo x; return; }
  printf '%s' "$s" | grep -Eq "^(npx[[:space:]]+)?($BIN_RUNNERS)([[:space:]]|\$)"                                  && { echo x; return; }
  printf '%s' "$s" | grep -Eq "^(npx[[:space:]]+)?playwright[[:space:]]+test([[:space:]]|\$)"                      && { echo x; return; }
  printf '%s' "$s" | grep -Eq "^(npx[[:space:]]+)?cypress[[:space:]]+(run|open)([[:space:]]|\$)"                   && { echo x; return; }
  # node's built-in test runner: `--test` may sit behind loader flags like
  # `--import tsx` (azure_private_agent/office does exactly this), so match
  # `--test`/`--experimental-test` ANYWHERE in the node arg list, not just
  # immediately after `node`. `--test-concurrency=` etc. don't match — the
  # flag must be followed by whitespace or end-of-segment.
  printf '%s' "$s" | grep -Eq "^node[[:space:]].*(--test|--experimental-test)([[:space:]]|\$)"                     && { echo x; return; }
  # tsx running node's test runner, incl. `npx tsx --test` / `npm exec tsx --test`.
  printf '%s' "$s" | grep -Eq "^(npm[[:space:]]+exec[[:space:]]+|npx[[:space:]]+)?tsx[[:space:]].*--test([[:space:]]|\$)" && { echo x; return; }
  # `next dev` (dev server) and `next build` (heavy prod build) both escape into
  # claude.slice when run bare — a bare `pnpm build`→`next build` + parallel
  # `tsc --noEmit` swap-thrashed every session for ~80min on 2026-06-18.
  printf '%s' "$s" | grep -Eq "^(npm[[:space:]]+exec[[:space:]]+|npx[[:space:]]+)?next[[:space:]]+(dev|build)([[:space:]]|\$)" && { echo x; return; }
  # Typecheck: `npm|pnpm|yarn run type-check` / `pnpm typecheck` and bare project
  # `tsc` (`tsc -p …`, `tsc -b`, `tsc --noEmit`). One `type-check` script is an
  # 8-project `tsc` chain — as heavy as a test pool — and N of them across
  # sessions CPU-starved every session on 2026-07-21 (load 47, RAM healthy).
  # Route to `capbuild`, which caps the run AND auto-serializes typechecks under
  # one shared lock so only one runs at a time. `tsc --version|help|init` are
  # trivial and exempt.
  printf '%s' "$s" | grep -Eq "^($PKG_RUNNERS)([[:space:]]+($PKG_FLAGS))*[[:space:]]+type-?check(:[^[:space:]]+)?([[:space:]]|\$)" && { echo x; return; }
  if printf '%s' "$s" | grep -Eq "^tsc([[:space:]]|\$)" \
     && ! printf '%s' "$s" | grep -Eq "^tsc[[:space:]]+--(version|help|init|showConfig)([[:space:]]|\$)"; then
    echo x; return
  fi
}

# Split on && || | ; & into one segment per line (longest operators first).
SEGMENTS=$(printf '%s' "$CMD" | sed -E 's/&&/\n/g; s/\|\|/\n/g; s/[;|&]/\n/g')

DANGER=""
while IFS= read -r seg; do
  # Trim leading subshell/brace punctuation and whitespace.
  seg=$(printf '%s' "$seg" | sed -E 's/^[[:space:](){}]*//')
  [ -z "$seg" ] && continue
  # NOTE: there is deliberately no `FORCE_BARE=1` bypass here. It is stripped
  # as an ordinary leading assignment below, so the underlying command is
  # judged on its merits. The human hatch lives in the interactive bashrc
  # wrappers, not on the agent's Bash-tool channel. (cf. 2026-06-11 incident)
  # Strip leading env-var assignments and an optional `env` prefix.
  while printf '%s' "$seg" | grep -Eq '^([A-Za-z_][A-Za-z0-9_]*=[^[:space:]]*[[:space:]]+|env[[:space:]]+)'; do
    seg=$(printf '%s' "$seg" | sed -E 's/^([A-Za-z_][A-Za-z0-9_]*=[^[:space:]]*[[:space:]]+|env[[:space:]]+)//')
  done
  # Strip a path prefix on the binary (./node_modules/.bin/vitest, /usr/bin/node).
  seg=$(printf '%s' "$seg" | sed -E 's#^([^[:space:]]*/)(pnpm|npm|yarn|turbo|bun|vitest|jest|mocha|ava|playwright|cypress|node|next|npx|tsx|tsc)([[:space:]]|$)#\2\3#')
  # Already-capped paths → safe. `slot` → dev.slice (dev servers); `capbuild`
  # → a hard-MemoryMax transient cgroup (one-shot builds/test suites).
  case "$seg" in slot\ *|capbuild\ *) continue ;; esac
  # systemd-run is safe ONLY if it targets a memory-capped slice; a bare
  # `--scope` lands in user.slice uncapped, which is the very escape we guard.
  if printf '%s' "$seg" | grep -Eq '^systemd-run([[:space:]]|$)'; then
    if printf '%s' "$seg" | grep -Eq -- '--slice[ =](dev|claude|test)\.slice'; then continue; fi
    DANGER="$seg"; break
  fi
  if [ -n "$(_is_bad "$seg")" ]; then DANGER="$seg"; break; fi
done <<< "$SEGMENTS"

[ -z "$DANGER" ] && exit 0

REASON='Refusing a bare dev-server / test-runner / typecheck / build from the Bash tool — it runs with no memory cap and can OOM or swap-thrash the box, and typechecks with no serialization CPU-starve every session (a bare vitest pool killed user@1000.service on 2026-06-07; stacked FORCE_BARE test loops froze every session on 2026-06-11; a bare `pnpm build`→`next build` + parallel `tsc --noEmit` swap-thrashed every session for ~80min on 2026-06-18; three concurrent `npm run type-check` chains drove load to 47 and froze every session on 2026-07-21 with RAM healthy). To run a test SUITE, TYPECHECK, or BUILD with a HARD memory cap and real output + exit code, prefix `capbuild`: e.g. `capbuild npm test`, `capbuild npm run type-check`, `capbuild npx tsc -p tsconfig.json --noEmit`, `capbuild node --test src/foo.test.ts`, `capbuild pnpm build`. capbuild auto-serializes typechecks (a shared `typecheck` lock), so concurrent ones queue instead of stampeding — only one runs at a time. For a DEV SERVER use `slot pnpm dev`. There is no unbounded path from the Bash tool by design — `FORCE_BARE=1` is not honored here (it only works for a human at an interactive shell prompt). Use `capbuild` and you get the same result, safely.'
printf '{"decision": "block", "reason": %s}\n' "$(printf '%s' "$REASON" | jq -Rs .)"
exit 0

#!/bin/bash
# PreToolUse hook for the Bash tool — shared-working-tree git hygiene +
# test-tier output integrity. Two rules that were CLAUDE.md prose until
# 2026-07-16, now mechanical (prose is advisory; hooks are deterministic):
#
# 1. Block `git add -A/--all` and `git commit -a/-am/--all`. Up to ~5 Claude
#    sessions share the main checkouts on this box; a blanket stage sweeps a
#    SIBLING session's uncommitted work into your commit (it nearly happened
#    landing ROADCODE 2026-07-15 — seven staged phase files sat in a sibling's
#    conflicted merge index). Stage explicit paths only.
# 2. Block piping a run-tier.sh test tier through truncating filters
#    (tail/head/grep/sed/awk/wc). Truncation eats the failure NAMES and costs
#    a full-tier rerun to recover each one; run-tier.sh already bounds stdout
#    and writes the full TAP stream to .test-logs/. `tee` is allowed (no loss).
#
# Fails OPEN if the command can't be read or jq is missing — a guard that
# can't parse must not wedge every Bash call (matches slot-test-guard).

INPUT=$(cat)
CMD=$(printf '%s' "$INPUT" | jq -r '.tool_input.command // empty' 2>/dev/null)
[ -z "$CMD" ] && exit 0

# Split into statements on && ; || (keep pipes inside a statement — rule 2
# needs to see them). Newlines count as separators too.
STATEMENTS=$(printf '%s' "$CMD" | tr '\n' ';' | sed -E 's/(\&\&|\|\||;)+/\n/g')

DENY=""
while IFS= read -r st; do
  [ -z "$st" ] && continue
  # Rule 1a: git … add … -A/--all   (short -A also inside bundles like -An is
  # not a thing for add; match -A/--all as standalone words)
  if printf '%s' "$st" | grep -Eq '(^|[[:space:]])git([[:space:]]+-C[[:space:]]+[^[:space:]]+)?([[:space:]]+[^[:space:]]+)*[[:space:]]+add([[:space:]]+[^[:space:]]+)*[[:space:]](-A|--all|--no-ignore-removal)([[:space:]]|$)'; then
    DENY="git add -A/--all stages a SIBLING session's uncommitted work on this shared tree. Stage explicit paths only: git add <file> <file>. (Rule: azure_private_agent CLAUDE.md §Shared working tree — mechanically enforced since 2026-07-16.)"
    break
  fi
  # Rule 1b: git … commit with -a / -am / --all (NOT --amend: two dashes + word)
  if printf '%s' "$st" | grep -Eq '(^|[[:space:]])git([[:space:]]+-C[[:space:]]+[^[:space:]]+)?([[:space:]]+[^[:space:]]+)*[[:space:]]+commit([[:space:]]+[^[:space:]]+)*[[:space:]](-a|-am|--all)([[:space:]]|$)'; then
    DENY="git commit -a/-am commits every tracked modification — including a sibling session's dirty files on this shared tree. Stage explicit paths, then commit without -a. (Rule: azure_private_agent CLAUDE.md §Shared working tree — mechanically enforced since 2026-07-16.)"
    break
  fi
  # Rule 2: run-tier.sh … | tail/head/grep/sed/awk/wc  (tee allowed)
  if printf '%s' "$st" | grep -Eq 'run-tier\.sh[^|]*\|[[:space:]]*(tail|head|grep|sed|awk|wc)([[:space:]]|$)'; then
    DENY="NEVER pipe a test tier through tail/head/grep — truncation eats the failure NAMES and costs a full-tier rerun to recover each one. run-tier.sh already bounds stdout (failure names + counts survive) and writes the full TAP stream to .test-logs/<slot>-<ts>.tap — read THAT for diagnostics. Run the tier bare (it self-wraps capbuild); \`| tee file\` is fine if you need a copy."
    break
  fi
done <<< "$STATEMENTS"

[ -z "$DENY" ] && exit 0
printf '{"decision": "block", "reason": %s}\n' "$(printf '%s' "$DENY" | jq -Rs .)"
exit 0

#!/bin/bash
# PreToolUse hook for the Bash tool — blocks the ugrep DFA-explosion pattern.
#
# THE HAZARD. Since Claude Code v2.1.117 the Bash-tool shell snapshot shadows
# `grep` with a shell FUNCTION that re-execs the ~300MB `claude.exe` binary as
# `ARGV0=ugrep ... -G` (ugrep 7.5.0 is embedded in the CLI; there is no `ugrep`
# on PATH). So a plain `grep` from the Bash tool is NOT GNU grep. Upstream bug:
# https://github.com/anthropics/claude-code/issues/54394 (open as of 2026-08-22).
#
# ugrep's default POSIX engine (RE/flex) compiles the pattern to a DFA BEFORE
# matching, and linear-time matchers must expand bounded repetitions away. Two
# counted repetitions over a wide character class around a literal make the DFA
# track the cross product of both counters — construction then allocates
# without bound: ~70-130 MB/s, no output, no termination, no SIGPIPE (it never
# emits a match, so a downstream `head` never kills it).
#
# 2026-08-22: Arwen ran
#     grep -o -i '[^<>]\{0,120\}retry[^<>]\{0,120\}' design.html
# on a 116KB minified HTML file (longest line 91,000 chars). One process reached
# 8.9G (rss+swap) inside the session's own scope, pushed it past MemoryHigh=8G
# with the 2G swap cap full, and livelocked the WHOLE cgroup — including the
# claude process — in mem_cgroup_handle_over_high for ~40 minutes. The session
# itself was innocent at ~800MB. GNU grep runs the identical pattern in 4.0s /
# 13MB and returns the right answer.
#
# THE DISCRIMINATOR (measured on that file, each in a hard-capped test.slice
# scope — see docs/host-gotchas.md for the full table):
#   [^<>]{0,120}retry[^<>]{0,120}   RUNAWAY      two wide bounds, both sides
#   .{0,120}retry.{0,120}           RUNAWAY      `.` counts as wide
#   \w{0,120}retry\w{0,120}         RUNAWAY
#   .{0,60}re.{0,60}try.{0,60}      RUNAWAY      three bounds
#   [^<>]{0,120}retry               ok    6MB    ONE bound is harmless
#   [0-9]{0,120}retry[0-9]{0,120}   ok    7MB    narrow class is harmless
#   [^<>]{0,25}retry[^<>]{0,25}     ok    7MB    small bound is harmless
#   bound sweep, both sides: {0,20} 6MB · {0,30} 184MB · {0,40}+ RUNAWAY
# So the trip is: >=2 counted repetitions whose max is >=32. Class width is NOT
# tested statically — it is not reliably decidable from the command text, and
# the false-positive cost is one extra flag while the false-negative cost is a
# frozen box. Deliberately NOT part of the rule: the alternation shape from
# issue #54394 (`"a":"[^"]*"|"b":"[^"]*"|...`) measured clean at 7MB here, so
# guarding it would be pure false-positive noise on this ugrep version.
#
# EXEMPT (all measured safe, all leave the caller a working escape):
#   -P / --perl-regexp   PCRE2 backtracks instead of building a DFA — 7MB
#   command grep         bypasses the function shim entirely
#   /bin/grep, /usr/bin/grep, any path-qualified grep — real GNU grep, 13MB
#   git grep             git's own matcher
#   rg / ripgrep         never matched here to begin with
# Only BARE `grep` is shimmed (the snapshot shadows exactly `find` and `grep`),
# so `egrep`/`fgrep` are real binaries and are not guarded.
#
# ANALYSIS IS WHOLE-COMMAND, NOT PER-SEGMENT. An earlier draft split on
# | && ; & and judged each segment. Three defects, all measured: a `;` or `&`
# INSIDE the pattern ([^&<>]{0,120}x[^&<>]{0,120}) split the counters apart and
# the runaway sailed through; a grep that is not the first word of its segment
# (`do grep`, `if grep`, `time grep`, a line continuation) was never examined;
# and the cost was ~7ms per line of command, 2.25s on a 300-line heredoc.
# Counting bounds across the whole command first is cheaper (one pass, exits in
# ~3 forks for the 99% case that has no large bounds at all) and strictly
# harder to evade. It over-approximates — a command with two large bounds
# somewhere and an unrelated grep elsewhere is treated as dangerous — which is
# the right direction to be wrong in, because the remedy is a safe rewrite.
#
# Fails OPEN if the command can't be read or jq is missing — a guard that
# cannot parse must not wedge every Bash call (matches slot-test-guard).

BOUND_MIN="${UGREP_GUARD_BOUND_MIN:-32}"   # a counted max >= this is "large"
COUNT_MIN="${UGREP_GUARD_COUNT_MIN:-2}"    # this many large counts = explosion
PREFIX_SIG='grep() { command '                # our own rewrite marker

INPUT=$(cat)
CMD=$(printf '%s' "$INPUT" | jq -r '.tool_input.command // empty' 2>/dev/null)
[ -z "$CMD" ] && exit 0

# Idempotence: never re-wrap our own output.
case "$CMD" in "$PREFIX_SIG"*) exit 0 ;; esac

# ── Fast path ───────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
# One pass over the whole command. Handles ERE `{0,120}` / `{120}` and BRE
# `\{0,120\}`; ignores open-ended `{5,}` (an unbounded loop needs no counter,
# so it cannot blow the DFA up). Almost every command exits here.
NBOUNDS=$(printf '%s' "$CMD" \
  | grep -oE '\\?\{[0-9]*(,[0-9]*)?\\?\}' \
  | sed -E 's/\\//g; s/[{}]//g' \
  | awk -F, -v min="$BOUND_MIN" '
      { max = (NF > 1 ? $2 : $1) }
      max ~ /^[0-9]+$/ && max + 0 >= min { c++ }
      END { print c + 0 }')
[ "${NBOUNDS:-0}" -ge "$COUNT_MIN" ] || exit 0

# ── Strip quoted spans and heredoc bodies ───────────────────────────
# Detection must look at words this shell will actually EXECUTE. A matcher
# name sitting inside a quoted payload or a heredoc is DATA, not an
# invocation: it belongs to `ssh host "..."`, `bash -c "..."`, a script being
# written with `cat > f <<EOF`, or a `herdr agent prompt` string. Judging
# those refused perfectly good commands - writing this hook's own test
# harness was blocked by this hook three times, which is how the
# false-positive rate got measured. The pattern text stays visible to the
# bound counter above (patterns ARE quoted); only the token and flag scanning
# below runs on the blanked text, so a real unquoted invocation is still
# caught. Quote state is carried ACROSS lines and honours backslash escapes
# inside double quotes, because a desync would blank real code and turn a
# false positive into a false NEGATIVE; heredoc terminators are matched
# allowing <<- tab-stripping and trailing whitespace. Fails open to the raw
# command if awk is unavailable.
BLANKED=$(printf '%s' "$CMD" | awk '
BEGIN { inh = 0; q = 0; qc = ""; dash = 0; ansic = 0 }
{
  line = $0
  if (inh) {
    t = line
    if (dash) { sub(/^[ \t]+/, "", t) }
    sub(/[ \t]+$/, "", t)
    if (t == term) inh = 0
    print ""; next
  }
  out = ""; n = length(line)
  for (i = 1; i <= n; i++) {
    c = substr(line, i, 1)
    # A backslash OUTSIDE quotes escapes the next character, so `echo it\'"'"'s`
    # never opens a string. Without this the apostrophe opened one awk-side that
    # bash never opened, and every following line was blanked — hiding a real
    # grep. Emitting the escaped char keeps `\grep` visible to detection.
    if (q == 0 && c == "\\") { out = out " " substr(line, i+1, 1); i++; continue }
    # A `#` starting a word begins a comment: the rest of the line is not code.
    # This matters because quote state is now carried ACROSS lines, so an
    # apostrophe in a comment ("# we don'"'"'t want ugrep here") would otherwise
    # open a string that swallows the remainder of the command.
    if (q == 0 && c == "#" && (i == 1 || substr(line, i-1, 1) ~ /[ \t;&|(]/)) { break }
    if (q == 1 && c == "\\" && (qc == "\"" || ansic)) { out = out "  "; i++; continue }
    if (q == 0 && (c == "'"'"'" || c == "\"")) { q = 1; qc = c; ansic = (c == "'"'"'" && i > 1 && substr(line, i-1, 1) == "$"); out = out " "; continue }
    if (q == 1 && c == qc)                        { q = 0; qc = ""; ansic = 0; out = out " "; continue }
    if (q == 1)                                   { out = out " "; continue }
    out = out c
  }
  if (q == 0 && match(out, /<<-?/)) {
    pos = RSTART + RLENGTH
    dash = (substr(out, RSTART, RLENGTH) ~ /-$/)
    if (substr(out, pos, 1) != "<") {
      rest = substr(line, pos)
      sub(/^[ \t]*/, "", rest)
      sub(/^[\047\"]/, "", rest)
      if (match(rest, /^[A-Za-z_][A-Za-z0-9_]*/)) {
        term = substr(rest, RSTART, RLENGTH); inh = 1
      }
    }
  }
  print out
}
' 2>/dev/null) || BLANKED="$CMD"
# `eval` is the one payload that is NOT data: it runs in THIS shell, so its
# quoted contents must stay visible to detection. Test the BLANKED text, not
# the raw command — an `eval` that is itself inside a heredoc (a deploy script
# being written) or inside an ssh payload is data like everything else, and
# keying off the raw text let it switch blanking off for the whole command.
if printf '%s' "$BLANKED" | grep -Eq '(^|[^A-Za-z0-9_.-])eval([[:space:]]|$)'; then
  BLANKED="$CMD"
fi
[ -n "$BLANKED" ] || BLANKED="$CMD"

# ── Which greps are in play? ────────────────────────────────────────────────
# Neutralise the invocations that never reach the shim, then see whether a bare
# `grep` word survives. Only a bare `grep` resolves to the shell function;
# `command grep`, `git grep` and any path-qualified grep are real matchers.
STRIPPED=$(printf '%s' "$BLANKED" | sed -E '
  s#(^|[^A-Za-z0-9_.-])(command[[:space:]]+grep|git[[:space:]]+grep)#\1_SAFEGREP_#g
  s#[A-Za-z0-9_./-]*/grep#_SAFEGREP_#g')
printf '%s' "$STRIPPED" | grep -Eq '(^|[^A-Za-z0-9_.-])grep([[:space:]]|$)' || exit 0

# Flag zone = from each bare `grep` up to the first quote OR shell
# metacharacter, whichever comes first — i.e. that grep's OWN argv and nothing
# else. Two distinct bugs are being avoided here. Stopping at the quote keeps
# the PATTERN TEXT out: without it `grep -o '.{0,120} -P .{0,120}'`
# false-exempts and `'.{0,120} -r .{0,120}'` false-trips the recursive branch
# (both measured). Stopping at a metacharacter keeps DOWNSTREAM COMMANDS out:
# with an unquoted pattern there is no quote to stop at, so the zone ran to
# end-of-line and `grep -oE PAT f | xargs -P 4 sh` false-exempted on xargs's
# -P, while an innocent later `ls -R` or `cp -r` false-tripped the veto.
ZONES=$(printf '%s' "$STRIPPED" | grep -oE '(^|[^A-Za-z0-9_.-])grep[^'"'"'"|;&<>()]*' || true)

# Recursive anywhere in the command => refuse; see the rewrite rationale below.
IS_RECURSIVE=0
printf '%s' "$ZONES" | grep -Eq -- '(^|[[:space:]])(-[A-Za-z]*[rR][A-Za-z]*|--recursive|--dereference-recursive)([[:space:]]|$)' && IS_RECURSIVE=1
# -d recurse / --directories=recurse walk directories exactly like -r, so
# they must veto the rewrite too — otherwise a recursive search gets its
# result set silently changed, which is the one outcome this hook refuses.
printf '%s' "$ZONES" | grep -Eq -- '(^|[[:space:]])(-d[[:space:]]*|--directories=)recurse' && IS_RECURSIVE=1

# Exempt only if EVERY bare grep already selects PCRE2 (no DFA, measured 7MB).
NZONES=$(printf '%s' "$ZONES" | grep -c . || true)
NPERL=$(printf '%s' "$ZONES" | grep -cE -- '(^|[[:space:]])(-[A-Za-z]*P[A-Za-z]*|--perl-regexp)([[:space:]]|=|$)' || true)
[ "${NZONES:-0}" -gt 0 ] && [ "${NPERL:-0}" -eq "${NZONES:-0}" ] && exit 0

# ── Remediation ─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
# Same principle as slot-test-guard -> capbuild: do not just refuse the work,
# route it somewhere safe. The difference is that a build is LEGITIMATELY heavy
# and needs a cgroup, whereas a grep is legitimately light — the weight here is
# purely a defect in one engine. So the safe route is not "run the broken thing
# in a box", it is "use the engine that is not broken": GNU grep answers the
# incident query in 0.4s at 13MB, against unbounded growth from ugrep.
#
# PreToolUse can rewrite the command (hookSpecificOutput.updatedInput), so the
# repair is applied FOR the caller rather than asked of them — no wasted turn,
# and it does not depend on the agent cooperating. Prepending a `grep()`
# function redefines the shim AFTER the shell snapshot has been sourced, so it
# wins for every grep in the command, including inside pipelines (verified).
# The Bash tool runs a FRESH bash per call, so the override cannot leak into a
# later call, and shell functions are not exported, so `xargs grep` /
# `find -exec grep` / `bash -c 'grep'` never reach the shim to begin with.
#
# THE REWRITE IS ALL-OR-NOTHING, AND RECURSION ANYWHERE VETOES IT. The prefix
# redefines `grep` for the WHOLE command, so it also converts any OTHER grep in
# the same command. The shim passes ugrep `--ignore-files --hidden
# --exclude-dir=.git`, and `--ignore-files` (gitignore awareness) has NO GNU
# equivalent — so converting an unrelated `grep -rn TODO src/` riding along in
# the same command silently starts matching inside .git/ and node_modules/.
# Measured: same command, ugrep 2 hits vs GNU 4 hits including .git and a
# vendored file. A silent change to a result set is worse than the memory bug
# this hook exists to prevent, so if ANY grep in the command is recursive the
# whole command is refused with guidance instead of rewritten.
#
# `-I` is part of the shim's flag set and is NOT a GNU default: without it GNU
# prints "binary file matches" and exits 0 where ugrep prints nothing and exits
# 1, which inverts `if grep -q ...`. So the rewrite pins `-I` to keep the exit
# status honest. (GNU supports -P too, so a mixed command containing a `-P`
# grep still rewrites correctly.)
GNU_GREP=""
for c in /bin/grep /usr/bin/grep; do [ -x "$c" ] && { GNU_GREP="$c"; break; }; done

WHY='`grep` from the Bash tool is NOT GNU grep. Claude Code (>=2.1.117) shadows it with a shell function that re-execs its own binary as the embedded ugrep, whose POSIX engine builds a DFA up front and expands counted repetitions. Two or more counted maxima over a wide class make it track the cross product and allocate WITHOUT BOUND — ~100MB/s, no output, and no SIGPIPE to stop it because it never emits a match, so a downstream `head` will not save you. On 2026-08-22 exactly this shape (`grep -o '"'"'[^<>]\{0,120\}retry[^<>]\{0,120\}'"'"' design.html` over a minified HTML file with a 91,000-char line) reached 8.9G in ONE process, blew past the session'"'"'s 8G MemoryHigh with its swap cap full, and livelocked the whole session cgroup for 40 minutes. Upstream: anthropics/claude-code#54394. Measured on that file: GNU grep 0.4s/13MB with the correct answer; ugrep unbounded. Single counted repetitions, narrow classes like [0-9], and maxima under 32 are all fine and are never touched here.'

if [ -n "$GNU_GREP" ] && [ "$IS_RECURSIVE" -eq 0 ]; then
  NEW_CMD="grep() { command $GNU_GREP -I \"\$@\"; }; $CMD"
  MSG="ugrep-guard: rerouted the grep(s) in this command to GNU grep ($GNU_GREP -I). $WHY Only the regex ENGINE changed, so the match result is the same; the one difference is binary files, which -I keeps skipped exactly as the shim does. Write it this way yourself next time: /bin/grep, -P, or rg."
  printf '%s' "$INPUT" | jq -c --arg c "$NEW_CMD" --arg m "$MSG" \
    '{hookSpecificOutput:{hookEventName:"PreToolUse",updatedInput:(.tool_input + {command:$c})},systemMessage:$m}'
  exit 0
fi

if [ "$IS_RECURSIVE" -eq 1 ]; then
  REASON="Refusing this command: it has two or more large counted repetitions AND a RECURSIVE grep. $WHY It is not auto-rerouted to GNU grep the way a single-file grep is, because the reroute redefines grep for the WHOLE command: the shim passes ugrep --ignore-files --hidden --exclude-dir=.git, and --ignore-files has no GNU equivalent, so a recursive grep would silently start matching inside .git/ and node_modules/ — a different result set, quietly. Pick explicitly: rg 'PATTERN' (respects ignore files, no DFA blowup) is usually what you want; or grep -rP if your pattern is PCRE-compatible, which keeps ugrep's exact file selection and only changes the regex dialect (note -P reads {0,120} as PCRE, so a BRE '"'"'\{0,120\}'"'"' becomes '"'"'{0,120}'"'"'); or $GNU_GREP -r with your own --exclude-dir flags. If the recursive grep is a separate, innocent part of a compound command, just run it as its own Bash call."
else
  REASON="Refusing a grep with two or more large counted repetitions, and no GNU grep was found at /bin/grep or /usr/bin/grep to reroute it to. $WHY Use rg, or add -P to select PCRE2 (which backtracks instead of building a DFA), rewriting any BRE '"'"'\{0,120\}'"'"' as '"'"'{0,120}'"'"'."
fi
printf '{"decision": "block", "reason": %s}\n' "$(printf '%s' "$REASON" | jq -Rs .)"
exit 0

Approval-gated setup for new repositories and gap-only standards work for
existing ones.

## Skills

- `using-zeroh-greenfield` chooses the correct workflow.
- `greenfield-init` interviews, proposes, waits for approval, and initializes.
- `brownfield-audit` identifies and fills approved gaps without replacing homes.
- `stack-decision` records sourced stack alternatives and the chosen option.

## Claude Code

```text
/plugin marketplace add Blade-Labs/zeroh-marketplace
/plugin install zeroh-greenfield@zeroh-marketplace
```

Restart Claude Code or begin a fresh session after installation so the skills are loaded.

```text
codex plugin marketplace add Blade-Labs/zeroh-marketplace
```

Install or enable `zeroh-greenfield` from the Codex plugin marketplace, then start a fresh Codex session.

 * Reusable greeting API. The CLI in ./cli.ts is a thin adapter over greet().
 */
export const DEFAULT_NAME = 'world'

/**
 * Build the greeting for `name`. Omitting `name` greets the default name.
 * @throws {TypeError} when `name` is given but is not a non-blank string.
 */
export function greet(name?: string): string {
  if (name === undefined) return `Hello, ${DEFAULT_NAME}!`
  if (typeof name !== 'string' || name.trim() === '') {
    throw new TypeError('greet: name must be a non-blank string')
  }
  return `Hello, ${name}!`
}
''')
create('src/cli.ts', r'''#!/usr/bin/env node
import { greet } from './index.ts'

const USAGE = [
  'Usage: greenfield-proof [name] [--help]',
  '',
  'Print a greeting for name (default: world).',
  '',
  'Options:',
  '  -h, --help  Show this usage and exit 0',
].join('\n')

interface CliResult {
  code: number
  stdout: string
  stderr: string
}

function run(argv: readonly string[]): CliResult {
  const positional: string[] = []
  for (const arg of argv) {
    if (arg === '--help' || arg === '-h') return { code: 0, stdout: USAGE + '\n', stderr: '' }
    if (arg.startsWith('-')) return { code: 1, stdout: '', stderr: 'Unknown option: ' + arg + '\n' + USAGE + '\n' }
    positional.push(arg)
  }
  if (positional.length > 1) return { code: 1, stdout: '', stderr: 'Too many arguments\n' + USAGE + '\n' }
  try {
    return { code: 0, stdout: greet(positional[0]) + '\n', stderr: '' }
  } catch (error) {
    const message = error instanceof Error ? error.message : String(error)
    return { code: 1, stdout: '', stderr: message + '\n' + USAGE + '\n' }
  }
}

const result = run(process.argv.slice(2))
process.stdout.write(result.stdout)
process.stderr.write(result.stderr)
process.exitCode = result.code
''')

## Conventions

- Keep the reusable API in `src/index.ts` and the thin executable adapter in `src/cli.ts`; publish only built artifacts through `exports`, `bin`, and `files`.

- Quality gates are bound in `roadmap/roadmap.config.json`; run them from the repository root exactly as configured.
- Product facts live in `docs/PRD.md`; stack and design rulings live in `docs/adr/`; the architecture index is `docs/architecture.md`; the CLI contract is `docs/ux-canon.md`.
- Commit subjects use `<type>(<scope>): <imperative summary>`.

## Don't

- Don't add a framework runtime, external service, authentication, mobile target, deployment, or product remote; this package is a library plus a local CLI.
- Don't invent design tokens, themes, or brand values; the package has no UI surface.
- Don't copy conventions into other harness files; they point here.
- Don't bypass a gate or downgrade a bound gate to `none` to make verification green.

## Generalize-forward

Extract a shared helper only when a second CLI option or API entry needs the same parsing or formatting; until then keep `src/index.ts` and `src/cli.ts` self-contained.

## Flag-first delivery

New behaviour ships behind an explicit option or exported function that defaults to today's behaviour; release-only work stays in `hold[]` until a release phase picks it up.

hold[]: none.

greenfield-proof: a small TypeScript reusable greeting API plus a CLI for developers. `greet(name?: string)` returns `Hello, <name>!`, defaults to `world`, and rejects blank names with a `TypeError`. The CLI prints the greeting, `--help` exits 0, and an unknown option exits 1 with usage.

Developers importing a greeting function and invoking its CLI.

## Platforms

Node 22+ on Linux. Mobile: none. No browser surface.

## Constraints

- npm is the package manager; the stack is tsup with TypeScript and node:test (ADR 0001).

- No framework runtime, external service, authentication, mobile target, deployment, or product remote.
- Non-Blade; design registry absent (ADR 0002).

## Non-goals

- Publishing to a registry.
- A UI, theme, or design tokens.
- Any network, service, or authentication behaviour.

## Success signals

The first release exports a typed greeting and CLI with passing tests: build, type check, unit tests, and the built CLI smoke check all exit 0. Adoption or usage measures: Don't know yet.

## Brand

Non-Blade. No brand values exist and none are invented.

- Keep the reusable API in `src/index.ts` and the thin executable adapter in `src/cli.ts`; publish only built artifacts through `exports`, `bin`, and `files`.
- Source is strict TypeScript (see `docs/CODE-STYLE.md`); imports between source files use explicit `.ts` extensions so Node runs them unbuilt.
- Behaviour tests live in `test/*.test.ts` and run with `node --test`; the built CLI smoke check is `node dist/cli.js --help`.
- Quality gates are bound in `roadmap/roadmap.config.json`; run them from the repository root exactly as configured.
- Product facts live in `docs/PRD.md`; stack and design rulings live in `docs/adr/`; the architecture index is `docs/architecture.md`; the CLI contract is `docs/ux-canon.md`.
- Commit subjects use `<type>(<scope>): <imperative summary>`.

## Don't

- Don't add a framework runtime, external service, authentication, mobile target, deployment, or product remote; this package is a library plus a local CLI.
- Don't invent design tokens, themes, or brand values; the package has no UI surface.
- Don't copy conventions into other harness files; they point here.
- Don't bypass a gate or downgrade a bound gate to `none` to make verification green.

## Generalize-forward

Extract a shared helper only when a second CLI option or API entry needs the same parsing or formatting; until then keep `src/index.ts` and `src/cli.ts` self-contained.

## Flag-first delivery

New behaviour ships behind an explicit option or exported function that defaults to today's behaviour; release-only work stays in `hold[]` until a release phase picks it up.

hold[]: none.
''')

## Visual language

None. greenfield-proof has no graphical surface; its only user-facing output is plain UTF-8 text on stdout and stderr. No fonts, palette, or spacing values exist and none are invented.

## Component vocabulary

- Greeting line: `Hello, <name>!` followed by a newline on stdout.
- Usage text: starts with `Usage: greenfield-proof [name] [--help]` and lists the options.
- Error line: one human-readable sentence followed by the usage text on stderr.

## Interaction rules

- `greenfield-proof` with no argument prints the default greeting and exits 0.
- `greenfield-proof <name>` prints the greeting for that name and exits 0.
- `--help` or `-h` prints the usage text on stdout and exits 0.
- An unknown option, more than one positional argument, or a blank name prints an error line plus the usage text on stderr and exits 1.
- Output is deterministic and never colored, interactive, or dependent on the terminal.

## Binding design system

None. Non-Blade with no UI surface; `designHomes.ux.bindingDesignSystem` is intentionally unset (ADR 0002).
''')

## Product

greenfield-proof: a small TypeScript reusable greeting API plus a CLI for developers. `greet(name?: string)` returns `Hello, <name>!`, defaults to `world`, and rejects blank names with a `TypeError`. ## Audience

Developers importing a greeting function and invoking its CLI.

## Platforms

Node 22+ on Linux. Mobile: none. No browser surface.

## Constraints

- npm is the package manager; the stack is tsup with TypeScript and node:test (ADR 0001).

- No framework runtime, external service, authentication, mobile target, deployment, or product remote.
- Non-Blade; design registry absent (ADR 0002).

## Non-goals

- Publishing to a registry.
- A UI, theme, or design tokens.
- Any network, service, or authentication behaviour.

The first release exports a typed greeting and CLI with passing tests: build, type check, unit tests, and the built CLI smoke check all exit 0. Adoption or usage measures: Don't know yet.

## Brand

Non-Blade. No brand values exist and none are invented.

## Decisions

| Date | Ruling | Reason |

- Adoption and usage measures beyond passing gates: Don't know yet.

create('docs/adr/0001-tech-stack.md', '''# ADR 0001: Technology stack

## Status

Accepted

## Date

2026-09-05

## Context

greenfield-proof is a small TypeScript reusable greeting API plus a CLI for developers, managed with npm, targeting Node 22+ on Linux, private and UNLICENSED with no publishing. It needs a bundler for `dist/` exports and a `bin`, a type check, and a test runner with minimal dependencies. No framework runtime, external service, authentication, mobile target, deployment, or product remote applies. The greeting API is an in-process library export, not a network API, so the Backend matrix was not presented.

## Options

### Library/CLI
| option | pros | cons | better when | component reuse | source |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| tsup + node:test | Compact bundling with built-in tests | Two separate tools | Small TypeScript package values minimal test dependencies | Exported modules and fixtures | tsup |
| tsdown + vitest | Modern bundling and rich tests | Additional test dependency | Vite-aligned libraries need fast test ergonomics | Exported modules and test helpers | tsdown |
| unbuild | Convention-led library output | Less explicit build control | Multi-format package follows unjs conventions | Package presets and modules | unbuild |

## Ruling

2026-09-05: tsup + node:test — selected for a small TypeScript package that values minimal test dependencies; tsup (https://tsup.egoist.dev/, MIT, Allowed anywhere) builds `src/index.ts` and `src/cli.ts` to ESM with declarations, and node:test (https://nodejs.org/api/test.html) runs behaviour tests without a test dependency.

Generator: the library-cli archetype's create-vite (https://vite.dev/guide/, MIT, Allowed anywhere), version 8.3.0 from the local npx cache and byte-verified against the published archive, template `vanilla-ts`, run into the repository root. Its web demo files were removed and `vite` was dropped from devDependencies because the package has no browser surface.

## Consequences

- Positive: one build tool, no test framework dependency, ESM-only output published through `exports`, `bin`, and `files`.
- Positive: source and tests run unbuilt under Node 22 type stripping, so `node --test` does not depend on `dist/`.
- Negative: no linter or formatter is installed; style is enforced only by the strict compiler flags recorded in `docs/CODE-STYLE.md`.
- Negative: `tsx` and `zod` are development dependencies solely for the roadmap emit tooling.

## Revisit when

A second output format, a browser target, or a test need beyond node:test assertions appears, or the package is scheduled for publishing.
''')

## Status

Accepted

## Date

2026-09-05

## Context

greenfield-proof is a library plus a command-line adapter with no user interface: its only surfaces are exported functions and text on stdout and stderr. It is non-Blade, so no sibling design handoff applies, and no brand values exist. Platforms: Node 22+ on Linux; mobile: none.

## Options
| option | pros | cons | better when | component reuse | source |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| shadcn/ui | Source-owned accessible components | Consumer maintains copied components | Tailored product UI needs full control | Components and registry items compose locally | https://ui.shadcn.com/docs |
| Radix Themes | Cohesive accessible component theme | Stronger visual conventions | Fast consistent UI matters more than source ownership | Theme primitives compose across screens | @radix-ui/themes |
| MUI | Broad mature component suite | Larger runtime and opinionated styling | Enterprise UI needs extensive ready-made widgets | Shared theme and component packages | @mui/material |

## Ruling

2026-09-05: No design system — the package has no UI surface, so none of the options applies; the selected registry is none, and no tokens, themes, fonts, palette, or spacing values are invented. The UX canon records the CLI text contract instead.

For Blade, store pointers only; tokens are owned by zeroh-design. Not applicable: this repository is non-Blade.

## Consequences

- Positive: no UI dependency, token home, or registry to maintain.
- Negative: if a UI surface is ever added, a design-system decision must be made from these options before any component is written.

## Revisit when

Any web, mobile, or terminal UI component beyond plain text output is proposed, or Blade branding is requested.

## Visual language

None. greenfield-proof has no graphical surface; its only user-facing output is plain UTF-8 text on stdout and stderr. No fonts, palette, or spacing values exist and none are invented.

## Component vocabulary

- Greeting line: `Hello, <name>!` followed by a newline on stdout.
- Usage text: starts with `Usage: greenfield-proof [name] [--help]` and lists the options.
- Error line: one human-readable sentence followed by the usage text on stderr.

## Interaction rules

- `greenfield-proof` with no argument prints the default greeting and exits 0.
- `greenfield-proof <name>` prints the greeting for that name and exits 0.
- `--help` or `-h` prints the usage text on stdout and exits 0.
- An unknown option, more than one positional argument, or a blank name prints an error line plus the usage text on stderr and exits 1.
- An unknown option always exits 1, even when `--help` or `-h` is also present in any position; help never masks an invalid invocation.
- Output is deterministic and never colored, interactive, or dependent on the terminal.

## Binding design system

None. Non-Blade with no UI surface; `designHomes.ux.bindingDesignSystem` is intentionally unset (ADR 0002).
